name: Colin Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the home farm at the Ashgrove Estate, which is sheep on the hill and potatoes and some wheat down in the valley. I start at seven, check the ewes on the quad bike, then whatever the farm manager, Gareth, has written on the whiteboard. Today it was fencing and grading seed potatoes. I'm the new boy at 58, which is a funny thing to be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there at 58?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a postman for thirty-one years. When they brought in the big sorting machines and the handheld scanners, the rounds got longer and the job got lonelier, and I took the voluntary package two years ago. Ruth, my wife, is a district nurse and said go and do something with your hands that you actually like. So here I am, learning to dag a sheep, which is cutting the mucky wool off its back end, and not very good at it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief, and go back to grading spuds. I'd probably make a joke at the pub quiz about all the money that went into chatbots that write bad poems. Then I'd say it's still worth keeping an eye on, because the post office didn't change overnight either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it means I get my last seven or eight working years as I pictured them. I'm a bit of a slow learner on the farm, and I'd like the time to actually get good at this. I'll admit part of me would be a little let down, because I do like a clever gadget once it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, three hill days and two in the potato shed. I'd use the chatbot on my phone now and then, like I do, to ask about foot rot or to draft a letter to the council about the potholes on our lane. Money-wise I'd change nothing, we're well set with my postal pension and Ruth's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, mostly, with a small bit of 'is that it?'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot now and then. Can you give me a recent example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a ewe was limping and I took a photo and asked the chatbot what it might be, and it said scald, which is a mild foot infection. Gareth said it was right, and he was a bit put out that the phone got there first. I'd keep doing that sort of thing, it's handy, but I wouldn't trust it with anything I couldn't check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that worries you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I lost one job to machines already and came out the other side with a decent payout and something better. If this is all AI amounts to, I've been lucky twice.

S0.say: I'd say that's a relief and get back to grading potatoes. I'd joke at the pub quiz about the money spent on chatbots that write bad poems, but say it's worth keeping an eye on.
S0.think: I get my last working years as I pictured them, with time to actually get good at farming. Part of me would be a little let down, because I like a clever gadget once it works.
S0.do: Keeps working three hill days and two in the potato shed, and keeps using a chatbot now and then for sheep questions and letters. Changes nothing about money, relying on his postal pension and his wife's income.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, with a small sense of anticlimax.
S0.quote: Gareth said it was right, and he was a bit put out that the phone got there first.
S0.fieldNote: Colin has already lived through one round of automation as a postman and came out well, which colours everything. He is wry and measured, and he uses AI tools in small, checkable ways. He sees the mild picture as a chance to finally get good at the farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the post office all over again, but everywhere at once. I'd say the gains need to be shared out, through tax on the companies, decent retraining and a shorter week, not all go to the shareholders. I'd post that on the local community page, and I'd get a few angry replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, I think I'd be fine. Sheep on a wet hill are a hard job for a robot for a good while yet, and I've got savings and a pension. The people I'd worry about are the young ones on the estate who've taken on mortgages thinking the work would always be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I did with the handheld scanners: let others go first, watch what works, then learn it properly. If the estate bought a grading machine with a camera that sorts the potatoes, I'd ask Gareth to put me on the training. I'd also join the farmworkers' union, which I haven't done yet, because the post office taught me you want that in place before the changes, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit watchful, like you are at lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own job do you think would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is the potato grading, because I'm frankly slow at it and a camera would beat me on day one. I'd ask to move up the hill more, with the flock. I'd rather be the one who knows the sheep than the one racing a machine down a belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the owners. How do you think they'd decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ashgrove is owned by a family who live in the city most of the year, and they make their decisions on spreadsheets. If a robot pays back in three years, they'll buy it, full stop. That's not wicked, it's just how they're set up, which is why I think the rules have to come from government.

S1.say: I'd say it's the post office all over again, but everywhere at once. The gains should be shared through company tax, retraining and a shorter week, not all go to shareholders.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, because sheep on a wet hill are hard for a robot and I've got savings and a pension. I'd worry about the young ones on the estate with fresh mortgages.
S1.do: Waits for others to try new machines, then asks to be trained on any camera grading machine the estate buys. Joins the farmworkers' union for the first time and asks to move more of his work onto the hill with the flock.
S1.feel: Calm and a little watchful, the way you are at lambing.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one who knows the sheep than the one racing a machine down a belt.
S1.fieldNote: He reads this picture through his postman years and expects to come through it. Although he leans left, he doesn't call the absentee owners wicked; he blames the rules and wants government to set them. Joining the union is a lesson he learned too late last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast for any society to handle fairly, and we need emergency measures, a basic income or something like it, straight away. I'd write to our member of parliament and I'd say it at the quiz, and I don't think people would laugh this time. I'd also say the companies making these things should be paying for the clean-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of work at sixty, two years early, and that part I can absorb. What frightens me is the whole country doing it at once. Ruth's a nurse, and if a robot can do her rounds too, our second income goes, and then the pension fund's shares go up and down like a yo-yo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd move a chunk of our savings out of shares and into plain cash and paying off the last bit on Ruth's car, so we're not exposed. I'd cancel the cruise we've half-booked for our 35th anniversary. Once it arrived, I'd sign on to every campaign going for a basic income and probably volunteer with the food bank in town, because I'd have time and they'd have queues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got a cushion, but anxious for everyone round me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What does that short a window take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing, it's not enough. With the scanners I had five years of rumours before the package came, and I used every month of it to plan. Two years is barely one lambing to the next and back again. You'd get to the end of the second year and the government would still be holding meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably as a chat in the kitchen, with Ruth there. I'd tell them we're all right, we've got the house and some money put by, and they shouldn't feel they have to send anything home. And I'd tell our younger one, Owen, who's an engineer, to start putting every spare penny away now, today.

S2.say: I'd say this is far too fast to handle fairly and we need emergency measures like a basic income straight away. The companies making these things should pay for the clean-up.
S2.think: Losing my job two years early at sixty I can absorb. What frightens me is the whole country going at once, my wife's nursing income going too, and our pension fund swinging wildly.
S2.do: Moves part of their savings from shares into cash, pays off his wife's car and cancels a half-booked anniversary cruise. After it arrives, campaigns for a basic income and volunteers at the town food bank.
S2.feel: Anxious for everyone around him, but not panicked, because he has a cushion.
S2.quote: Two years is barely one lambing to the next and back again.
S2.fieldNote: His comparison point is the five years of rumours before his postal job went, which he used to plan. Here the speed, not the end point, is what unsettles him. He acts both for his household, shifting money to cash, and for others, through campaigning and the food bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a few years, so let's use them, and I'd be properly vocal about a basic income and about taxing robots. I'd tell people at work to get in the union now. And I'd say, look, I've been through this once, it's survivable if you plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years puts me at 63, which is about when I'd have stopped anyway. So for me it mostly means stopping on time rather than on my own terms. My real worry would still be Ruth's job and our boys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Ashgrove and learn whatever new kit came in, because it'd keep me useful and I'd find it interesting. I'd move some savings to cash over the five years rather than in a rush. And I'd join a campaign group, the sort that goes round town halls, because five years is long enough for that sort of thing to actually change a law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. Like a long forecast of rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, you'd see it coming. Would you use that time to learn the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more or less. I'd have a few months a year to learn how the robots work, and I'd probably enjoy that. If the estate put in a robot that checks the ewes on the hill with a drone and a camera, I'd want to be the one who reads its reports for Gareth. That might even stretch my job out a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a plan, or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much that. I'm not going to become a robot engineer at 60, I know my limits. But I could be the bloke who knows the hill and the sheep and can tell when the machine's got it wrong.

S3.say: I'd say we've been given a few years, so let's use them, and push hard for a basic income and a tax on robots. I'd tell people at work to join the union now.
S3.think: Five years puts me at 63, about when I'd have stopped anyway, so for me it means stopping on time rather than on my own terms. My real worry is my wife's job and our sons.
S3.do: Keeps working at the estate and learns any new kit, hoping to read a drone's flock reports for the manager. Moves some savings to cash gradually and joins a campaign group that tours town halls.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but in a way he can live with, like a long forecast of rain.
S3.quote: I could be the bloke who knows the hill and the sheep and can tell when the machine's got it wrong.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he shifts from defence to quiet adaptation, picturing himself as the person who checks the machine. He is honest about his limits and calls his plan half hope. The campaigning becomes more patient and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrapheap, and I'd keep saying it. I'd say the young ones should start planning now. And I'd probably say, with a grin, that I'll be watching it from a deckchair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't touch me much. I'd be 68, retired five years, probably arguing with the robot about how to plant my runner beans. I'd be thinking about Owen and his brother, who'll be in their forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am at Ashgrove until 63 or so, and learn what I need to as things change. I wouldn't change our money plans at all. I'd nudge the boys, more than once probably, to keep some savings in cash and to think about what in their work a machine can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, even. I'd like to see what it looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sons over those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as I'm saying now, they'd hear it at Christmas for ten years. Owen says engineers will be fine, and maybe they will. But I said the same about postmen in 1995.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you believe this one would really happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want to see it work. I've seen enough machines that were going to change everything to know they mostly change something. If it really does come, I'll be glad I was out of the way, and sorry for the ones who weren't.

S4.say: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrapheap. I'd tell the young ones to plan now, and joke that I'd watch from a deckchair.
S4.think: It doesn't touch me much, because I'd be 68 and retired. I'd be thinking about my sons, who'll be in their forties by then.
S4.do: Carries on at the estate until about 63, learning what he needs as things change, and leaves his money plans alone. Nudges his sons, repeatedly, to keep cash savings and think about what in their work a machine can't do.
S4.feel: Calm and curious about what the world will look like.
S4.quote: Owen says engineers will be fine, and maybe they will. But I said the same about postmen in 1995.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture lands after his planned retirement, so he is curious rather than worried. He doubts it will fully happen but takes it seriously enough to warn his sons. His sharpest line turns his own past against his son's confidence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can handle my own end of it, but everyone at once, nurses and engineers and farm lads, with no time for the government to catch up, that's how you get real hardship. What would help is a basic income ready to switch on, paid for by taxing the firms that own the machines, so nobody's left choosing between the gas bill and food.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd do it all again. I would. Losing the post round was the best bad thing that happened to me. And I think people can come through these changes if someone's got their back while they do.

headlineQuote: Losing the post round was the best bad thing that happened to me.
portrait: Colin Zhang is 58, a former postman who took voluntary redundancy when sorting machines and scanners changed his job, and now works as a junior hand on the Ashgrove Estate's sheep and potato farm. He's wry, measured and uses a chatbot now and then for small, checkable things. Having come through one round of automation, he stays calm in the milder pictures and expects to be fine personally. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, not for himself but for his wife's nursing income, his sons and the country as a whole. He wants gains shared through taxes on the machine owners and a basic income.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because everyone would be hit at once with no time for government to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income ready to switch on, paid for by taxing the firms that own the machines, so nobody has to choose between heating and food.
